title: The Queen of Sheba and the Splendor of Solomon
summary: The queen of Sheba travels to Jerusalem to test Solomon with hard questions, finds his wisdom and court beyond anything she was told, and praises the LORD who made him king to do justice and righteousness. The chapter then catalogs Solomon's staggering wealth: yearly gold, golden shields, an ivory throne, a trading fleet, and a large force of chariots and horses bought from Egypt and Kue.
story: This is the summit of Solomon's reign, and it comes right before the fall. In chapter 3 Solomon asked for wisdom and God promised riches and honor besides; here the promise is visibly kept, and a foreign ruler says aloud what the narrator wants us to see: the LORD loves Israel and set this king on the throne to do justice. The scene also fulfills, in a small way, the hope of Solomon's prayer in 8:41-43, that foreigners would hear of the LORD's great name and come. Yet the second half of the chapter, with its heaps of gold and its horses from Egypt, reads differently to anyone who knows Deuteronomy's law of the king, and it prepares directly for chapter 11, where Solomon's heart turns.
historical:
Sheba (Saba) was a kingdom in southwestern Arabia, in the region of modern Yemen, whose wealth came from frankincense, myrrh, and other aromatics carried north by caravan to Egypt, the Levant, and Mesopotamia. Inscriptions from Saba itself come mostly from later centuries, and no text outside the Bible names this queen, so her historical identity cannot be checked. Arabian women rulers are, however, attested in Assyrian records of the eighth century BC, and a visit to a king who controlled the northern ends of the trade routes makes good commercial sense. Later traditions attached many stories to her, including the Ethiopian royal tradition that traces its line to her and Solomon, but those stories are not in the text.

Kue (verse 28) is usually identified with Cilicia in southeastern Asia Minor, a region known for horses, and the Hittites and Aram of verse 29 are the small kingdoms of Syria. The picture is of Solomon as a middleman in the horse and chariot trade between Egypt and the north. The ships of Tarshish (verse 22) were large seagoing vessels; the phrase probably names a class of ship, and the location of Tarshish itself is debated, with Tartessos in Spain the most common suggestion.
cultural:
Testing a ruler with riddles or hard questions was a recognized form of courtly contest in the ancient world, a way to measure a king's wisdom and so his worth as a partner. The queen's gifts and Solomon's return gifts (verses 10 and 13) were the formal exchange of diplomacy, and verse 15 hints that trade agreements lay underneath the visit. Her amazement at the food, the seating of officials, the servants' clothing, and the cupbearers shows what ancient courts displayed: order and abundance as signs of a well-governed realm.

The weights are enormous. A talent was roughly 30 kilograms, so 666 talents a year would be about twenty tons of gold. The throne with its six steps and twelve lions used royal lion imagery common across the Near East, and the twelve lions may echo the twelve tribes. Some of the imported goods are hard to identify: almug wood (perhaps a type of sandalwood) is unknown, and the Hebrew word translated peacocks is uncertain; some translate it baboons. Readers sometimes connect the 666 talents with the number in Revelation 13:18, but nothing in either text requires the link.
literary: The chapter has two panels. Verses 1-13 are a story built on seeing and hearing: the queen hears (verse 1), sees (verse 4), says the report she heard was true (verse 6), and did not believe until she saw (verse 7). Her speech in verses 6-9 is the theological center, praising not Solomon but the LORD. A parenthesis in verses 11-12 about Hiram's fleet interrupts the story, a sign of the book's use of archival notes. Verses 14-29 are an inventory marked by superlatives: nothing like it was ever made (verse 20), silver was counted as nothing (verse 21), Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth (verse 23). Read beside Deuteronomy 17:16-17, which forbids a king to multiply horses, send people back to Egypt for them, take many wives, or pile up silver and gold, the list becomes a quiet charge sheet. The chapter admires and warns in the same breath.

outline.t: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon
Her verdict: praise to the LORD who made him king
Gifts exchanged; almug wood from Ophir
Gold shields, an ivory throne, and the ships of Tarshish
The whole world seeks Solomon's wisdom
Chariots, horses, and trade with Egypt and Kue

doctrines.note: Solomon's wisdom is presented as God's gift, the wisdom God had put in his heart (verse 24). It shows itself in answering hard questions and in ordering a kingdom well, and its purpose, in the queen's words, is justice and righteousness.

A foreign ruler comes because of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD and ends by blessing Israel's God. The scene shows Israel's calling to be a people through whom the nations come to know the LORD.

The queen names the purpose of kingship: God made Solomon king to carry out justice and righteousness. Wealth and splendor are not the goal of the office, and the chapter's inventory tests Solomon against that purpose.

words.note: Chidah, riddle or hard question. The word covers riddles (Samson's in Judges 14), enigmatic sayings, and difficult questions. It is also used for the puzzling sayings of the wise in Proverbs 1:6. The queen came to probe the depth of Solomon's understanding, not to trade pleasantries.

Chokmah, wisdom. In the Old Testament wisdom is skill for living, from craftsmanship to governing to moral judgment, rooted in the fear of the LORD. It appears six times in this chapter, which makes wisdom, not wealth, the chapter's stated subject.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. Paired with mishpat (justice) in verse 9, it describes right relationships kept faithfully, especially a ruler's protection of the weak. The pairing is the prophets' standard for kings, and Kings measures Solomon by it.

christ: Jesus referred to this chapter directly. He said the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom and would rise at the judgment to condemn his own generation, because something greater than Solomon was now present (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31). The point was not that Jesus was richer or cleverer, but that the wisdom Solomon received as a gift, Jesus is; Paul later calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The scene of nations bringing gifts to a son of David also shapes later hopes, such as Isaiah 60 and Psalm 72, which Christians have seen answered as the Gentiles come to Christ. Those links are thematic: the chapter describes Solomon, and the New Testament reads it as a picture of a greater king.

hard.q: Is this chapter praising Solomon's wealth, and is it believable?
hard.a:
Two questions are tangled here. On the first, interpreters differ in emphasis. Some read the chapter as straightforward celebration of God's promise in 3:13 coming true. Others note that its details (gold heaped up, horses from Egypt, and in the next chapter many wives) match item by item the things Deuteronomy 17:16-17 forbids a king, and they read the praise as deliberately double-edged. Both readings take the text seriously, and the second explains why chapter 11 follows so abruptly.

On the second, some historians regard the figures as exaggerated court language, pointing to the modest size of Jerusalem in the tenth century BC as it appears in current excavations. Others reply that ancient royal inscriptions report comparable quantities of gold, that Jerusalem's tenth-century remains are hard to excavate beneath later cities, and that a king who taxed a trade corridor could grow rich quickly. The chapter's theological claim does not depend on settling the exact tonnage.

questions: The queen said she did not believe until she came and saw. What moved you, or might move you, from hearing about God to seeing for yourself?
Her praise turns from Solomon to the LORD. How can people who admire what you do be pointed past you to God?
The chapter lists good gifts that became dangers. Where might abundance, rather than scarcity, be the greater test for you?
